content: 1. Over time, sedentary behaviors such as playing video games, using computers, and prolonged sedentary bouts have been associated with higher cardiometabolic risk in six studies, while two studies reported lower risk. 2. Four studies utilized data from the Quebec Adiposity and Lifestyle Investigation in Youth study, and two studies used data from the German Health Interview and Examination Survey for Children and Adolescents. 3. The quality of evidence for cross-sectional studies was downgraded from low to very low due to serious risk of bias and inconsistency. 4. Regarding bone health and sedentary behavior in children and adolescents, the association between sedentary behavior and health-related outcomes was examined, including whether a dose-response relationship exists based on total volume, frequency, duration, and intensity of interruptions. 5. The population studied included children aged 5 to under 18 years. Greater sedentary behavior volume and reduced frequency, duration, or intensity of interruptions were compared to lesser sedentary behavior volume and increased interruptions. 6. Bone health outcomes were deemed critically important but were not reviewed in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children and Young People. 7. Evidence from observational studies on sedentary behavior and bone health in children and adolescents was limited. Lower extremity bone outcomes showed a consistent negative association with objectively measured total sedentary time, independent of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (MVPA). 8. No association was observed between total sedentary time and lumbar spine bone outcomes, while total body bone outcomes showed no consistent association with sedentary time. 9. Limited evidence suggests that sedentary behavior is not related to bone health in children and adolescents. The PAGAC grade for this evidence was limited. 10. Sedentary behavior and body composition in children and adolescents were also examined. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with unfavorable body composition, particularly for screen time and television viewing, compared to total sedentary time. 11. Accelerometer-derived sedentary time was associated with unfavorable body composition in five out of 18 studies, while screen time and television viewing were associated with unfavorable outcomes in 15 out of 17 and 15 out of 18 studies, respectively. 12. Evidence for computer use and video game time was less consistent, with only three out of five studies and zero out of two studies, respectively, showing associations with unfavorable body composition. 13. Higher sedentary behavior was associated with better body composition in one out of nine studies for accelerometer-derived sedentary time. 14. Limited evidence suggests that greater sedentary behavior is related to higher weight status or adiposity in children and adolescents, with stronger evidence for television viewing or screen time than for total sedentary time. 15. Adverse effects of sedentary behavior in children and adolescents were also explored, but no systematic reviews or GRADE evidence profiles were identified by WHO or the Australian guidelines. 16. Mental health outcomes related to sedentary behavior in children and adolescents were also examined, focusing on associations with health-related outcomes and potential dose-response relationships.
